constellation-001.summary: A fall zodiac constellation depicting the owner of the Golden Fleece that Jason set out to find.
facts: Some 2,000 years ago the vernal equinox lay here, which made it the first sign of the zodiac.
It's the birth sign for late March to mid-April, but at that time of year the Sun actually sits in Pisces.

constellation-002.summary: A winter zodiac constellation depicting the form Zeus took to carry Europa across the sea.
facts: The red star set in the bull's eye is an aging giant about 67 light-years away.
A V-shaped star cluster forms the bull's face, and the Pleiades mark its shoulder.

constellation-003.summary: A winter zodiac constellation depicting the brothers Castor and Pollux, sons of Zeus and Leda.
facts: Castor is the alpha star, but Pollux is actually a little brighter.
Around December 13–14, a meteor shower of more than 100 meteors an hour streams from here.

constellation-004.summary: A spring zodiac constellation depicting the creature that bit Heracles' foot while he fought the Hydra, and was killed for it.
facts: Even its brightest star is only magnitude 3.5, so it's hard to spot under city lights.
The Beehive Cluster at its center is the group that Galileo Galilei's telescope split into some 40 stars.

constellation-005.summary: A spring zodiac constellation shaped like the crouching beast of Nemea that Heracles strangled with his bare hands.
facts: The stars of its head form a sickle, like a backward question mark.
Every mid-November the Leonid meteor shower pours out from here.

constellation-006.summary: A spring zodiac constellation depicting a goddess holding an ear of grain.
facts: The blue star at the ear of grain sits at the end of the great Spring Arc.
It's the second largest of the 88 constellations, and a cluster of some 1,300 galaxies lies in its direction.

constellation-007.summary: A summer zodiac constellation depicting the scales held by the goddess of justice.
facts: It's said to be named for the scales because the Sun stood here at the autumn equinox, when day and night are equal.
In ancient Greece it was seen as the scorpion's claws, and it's the only one of the 12 zodiac signs that is an object rather than a living thing.

constellation-008.summary: A summer zodiac constellation with its tail curled into an S and its stinger raised.
facts: The red star at its heart means “rival of Mars,” and it also appears on the flag of Brazil.
Because it felled Orion with its sting, legend says the two were placed on opposite sides of the sky, so one sets as the other rises.

constellation-009.summary: A summer constellation depicting a centaur drawing a bow.
facts: In traditional Korean astronomy, its six dipper-shaped stars were called Namduyukseong, the Southern Dipper.
In the West these stars are seen as a teapot, and just above its spout lies the center of the Milky Way.

constellation-010.summary: A fall zodiac constellation shaped like a horned beast in front with a fish's tail behind.
facts: It's said to be the god Pan, caught halfway through a transformation as he leapt into the water to escape the monster Typhon.
The Tropic of Capricorn got its name because, in ancient times, the Sun stood here at the winter solstice.

constellation-011.summary: A fall zodiac constellation depicting Ganymede, the handsome youth who served as Zeus's cupbearer.
facts: The stream of water it pours flows into Piscis Austrinus.
In 2017, its star TRAPPIST-1 was found to have seven Earth-sized planets.

constellation-012.summary: A fall zodiac constellation depicting two sea creatures whose tails are tied together with a cord.
facts: It's said to be Aphrodite and Eros, who changed shape to escape the monster Typhon.
Today's vernal equinox lies inside it, not in Aries.

constellation-013.summary: A winter constellation shaped like a hunter wearing three stars in a row on his belt.
facts: Betelgeuse at his shoulder is red, while Rigel at his foot is blue.
Follow the three belt stars down to the left and you reach Sirius, the brightest star in the night sky.

constellation-014.summary: A winter constellation depicting the larger of the two hunting animals that follow Orion the hunter.
facts: The brightest star in the night sky, about 8.6 light-years away, is found here.
Because the hot weather arrived when that star rose with the Sun, Westerners called midsummer the “dog days.”

constellation-015.summary: A winter constellation depicting the smaller of the two hunting animals that follow Orion the hunter.
facts: Its brightest star, Procyon, means “before the dog,” since it rises ahead of Sirius.
It forms one corner of the Winter Triangle.

constellation-016.summary: A winter constellation drawn as a pentagon, showing a man holding the reins with a young goat in his arms.
facts: Its brightest star, the sixth brightest in the night sky, marks the northern corner of the Winter Hexagon.
One corner star of the pentagon was once shared with neighboring Taurus.

constellation-017.summary: A winter constellation depicting a small creature crouched at the hunter's feet, chased by his hounds.
facts: It lies just south of Orion and west of Canis Major, low in the southern winter sky.
It holds a red star that Hind described in 1845 as looking like “a drop of blood on a black field.”

constellation-018.summary: A long winter constellation depicting the river that Phaethon fell into after losing control of the Sun chariot.
facts: It winds from Orion's feet all the way to the far south and is the sixth largest of the 88 constellations.
Achernar, at the river's end, never rises north of latitude 33° N, so it's hard to see from South Korea.

constellation-019.summary: A large constellation of the northern spring sky that holds seven stars shaped like a dipper.
facts: Extend the line through the two stars at the end of the dipper five times and you reach Polaris.
It's the third largest of the 88, and its seven dipper stars on their own are called the Big Dipper.

constellation-020.summary: A small dipper-shaped constellation with Polaris at the tip of its tail.
facts: Polaris sits at almost the same height as the local latitude, so in Seoul it stands about 37° above the horizon.
The star at the tip of the tail barely moves, which makes it useful for finding direction.

constellation-021.summary: A spring constellation drawn in the shape of a kite, showing a man herding and chasing the bears.
facts: Follow the curve of the Big Dipper's handle down and you reach its orange star.
The 1933 Chicago World's Fair switched on its opening lights using light captured from its brightest star.

constellation-022.summary: A spring constellation depicting the two hunting dogs led by the herdsman.
facts: Its stars are faint, but the Whirlpool Galaxy lies in its direction.
Its brightest star, Cor Caroli, means “Charles's heart” and honors an English king.

constellation-023.summary: A southern spring constellation whose four stars form a small trapezoid.
facts: Legend says that, sent by Apollo to fetch water, it stopped to eat figs, lied about it, and was punished.
Extend the line joining the trapezoid's two northern stars and you reach Spica in Virgo.

constellation-024.summary: A spring constellation depicting the many-headed monster slain by Heracles.
facts: It stretches more than 100° from head to tail, spanning over a quarter of the sky.
It's the largest of the 88, yet its only bright star is its alpha star, whose name means “the solitary one.”

constellation-025.summary: A summer constellation depicting the stringed instrument Hermes made from a tortoise shell and Orpheus played.
facts: Its brightest star is Vega, the Weaver Girl star who meets the Cowherd on Chilseok, the seventh night of the seventh lunar month.
It forms the brightest corner of the Summer Triangle.

constellation-026.summary: A summer constellation depicting the bird that carried Zeus's thunderbolts, its wings spread beside the Milky Way.
facts: Its brightest star, Altair, the Cowherd star, spins once in under 8 hours, so it bulges at the equator.
It faces Lyra across the Milky Way.

constellation-027.summary: A summer constellation depicting the bird Zeus turned into, its wings spread along the Milky Way.
facts: Its large cross shape also earns it the name Northern Cross.
The star at its tail is one corner of the Summer Triangle.

constellation-028.summary: A summer constellation showing a club-wielding hero kneeling upside down.
facts: Four stars in its middle form a keystone.
It holds the globular cluster often ranked the finest in the Northern Hemisphere sky.

constellation-029.summary: A summer constellation depicting the god of medicine gripping a snake in both hands.
facts: It straddles the ecliptic but isn't one of the 12 zodiac signs.
The supernova that appeared here in 1604 was recorded in the “Annals of the Joseon Dynasty” four days before Johannes Kepler noted it.

constellation-030.summary: A summer constellation depicting the animal said to have rescued the musician Arion by carrying him on its back after he leapt into the sea.
facts: Two of its stars were named in 1814 by an assistant at the Palermo Observatory, who spelled his own Latin name backward.
In the West its four diamond-shaped stars are called “Job's Coffin.”

constellation-031.summary: A northern constellation depicting a queen punished for boasting that her daughter was lovelier than the sea nymphs.
facts: When the Big Dipper sinks below the horizon, this constellation is used to find Polaris instead.
Its five stars form a W, which appears upside down when it climbs above Polaris on winter nights.

constellation-032.summary: A northern constellation depicting the king, husband of Queen Cassiopeia, drawn in the shape of a pentagonal house.
facts: Its brightest star will take over as the pole star around the year 7500.
Cepheid variables, named after its Delta star, became a yardstick for measuring distances across the universe.

constellation-033.summary: A northern constellation depicting the monster that guarded the golden apples of the Hesperides and was killed by Heracles.
facts: It winds between Ursa Major and Ursa Minor.
When the pyramids of Egypt were being built, its star Thuban served as the pole star.

constellation-034.summary: A fall constellation depicting the winged horse born from Medusa's blood.
facts: In 1995 the first planet found orbiting a Sun-like star was discovered here, a find that won a Nobel Prize in 2019.
Of the four stars that make up the Great Square of fall, one actually belongs to Andromeda.

constellation-035.summary: A fall constellation depicting the princess chained to a rock as an offering to a sea monster.
facts: It looks like two strands of stars streaming out from the Great Square of fall.
A neighboring galaxy visible to the naked eye lies within it.

constellation-036.summary: A fall constellation depicting a hero holding up a monster's head.
facts: Around August 12–13, in the middle of summer vacation, a meteor shower streams from this direction.
Algol, the star marking Medusa's head, dims and brightens again about every 2.9 days.

constellation-037.summary: A fall constellation depicting the sea monster that tried to devour a princess.
facts: Mira, whose name means “wonderful,” fades from naked-eye view and reappears about every 11 months.
It's the fourth largest of the 88 constellations, but with few bright stars it's hard to find.

constellation-038.summary: A fall constellation shown drinking the water that pours from a water pitcher.
facts: A single bright star shines on its own in the southern fall sky.
That star's name means “mouth of the fish.”

constellation-039.summary: A constellation of the southern sky depicting the keel of the ship Argo.
facts: The second brightest star in the night sky lies here.
Seen low on the southern horizon from Jeju, that star was known as the “Old Man of the South Pole.”

constellation-040.summary: A large constellation of the southern sky depicting a creature that is half human, half horse.
facts: The star closest to the Sun lies in this direction.
It wraps around Crux on three sides, and Crux was counted as part of it until the late 16th century.

constellation-041.summary: A small constellation whose long axis, extended, points to the south celestial pole, making it a guide across the Southern Hemisphere.
facts: It's the smallest of the 88 constellations, about one-twentieth the size of Hydra.
It appears on the flags of Australia, New Zealand, Brazil, Papua New Guinea and Samoa.

constellation-042.summary: A constellation of the southern sky depicting a peacock with its tail fanned out.
facts: It was created from observations made by navigators from the Netherlands in the 1590s.
Its brightest star got the name Peacock in the 1930s, when the United Kingdom's Royal Air Force was compiling a navigation almanac.

constellation-043.summary: A constellation of the southern sky depicting a firebird that comes back to life.
facts: Its brightest star, Ankaa, takes its name from the Arabic word for the firebird.
It hangs briefly low in the southern sky in fall.

constellation-044.summary: A cloud where new stars are being born, hanging just below the hunter's belt.
facts: Although it's about 1,300 light-years away, it shows up to the naked eye as a hazy patch in Orion's sword.
At its center, four young stars are grouped in a trapezoid.

constellation-045.summary: A nebula where a dark pillar of dust shaped like an animal's head blocks out a bright red cloud behind it.
facts: It gives off no light of its own; its shape stands out because it blocks the light behind it.
It lies close to the belt stars of Orion.

constellation-046.summary: An expanding cloud of debris from a star that exploded in 1054.
facts: Records from Song dynasty China and from Japan describe that year's “guest star.”
The neutron star at its center spins nearly 30 times a second.

constellation-047.summary: A cluster of young stars twinkling like a scatter of millet grains on the bull's shoulder.
facts: As noted in the “Dongguk Sesigi,” Koreans called it Myoseong or Jomsaengi-byeol.
Subaru, the carmaker from Japan, took both its name and its six-star emblem from this cluster.

constellation-048.summary: A loose cluster of stars forming the V of the bull's face.
facts: It's considered the closest open cluster to Earth.
The red star at the tip of the V isn't actually part of the cluster.

constellation-049.summary: A neighboring spiral galaxy that is among the most distant objects visible to the naked eye.
facts: It's about 2.5 million light-years away, so the light we see today set out 2.5 million years ago.
The odds of it colliding with the Milky Way within the next 10 billion years are put at roughly 50-50.

constellation-050.summary: A sky object where two star clusters sit side by side in a single field of view.
facts: It lies within Perseus, close to Cassiopeia.
Both clusters are faintly visible even to the naked eye.

constellation-051.summary: A summer planetary nebula that looks like a donut with a hole in the middle.
facts: It lies between the Beta and Gamma stars of Lyra, south of Vega.
It's the shell of gas thrown off by a dying star.

constellation-052.summary: A red nebula divided into three by dark lanes of dust.
facts: It sits in the Milky Way toward Sagittarius, right next to the Lagoon Nebula.
Its name means “split into three.”

constellation-053.summary: A ball of hundreds of thousands of old stars packed together in the summer sky.
facts: Through binoculars it looks like a round tuft of cotton, and under very dark skies it's barely visible to the naked eye.
The Arecibo radio message was beamed toward it in 1974 and will take about 25,000 years to arrive.

constellation-054.summary: A red nebula spread out in a shape that resembles a map of a continent.
facts: It lies right beside Deneb in Cygnus but usually can't be seen with the naked eye.
Its shape only shows clearly in photographs.

constellation-055.summary: A spring galaxy with sharply defined, tightly wound spiral arms.
facts: One of its arms can be seen linking it to a smaller galaxy.
In 1845 it became the first object whose spiral structure was recognized, by the Earl of Rosse.

constellation-056.summary: A galaxy seen edge-on that looks like a wide-brimmed hat.
facts: A dark lane of dust across its middle looks like the brim.
Its center is thought to hold a black hole of about 600 million to 1 billion times the mass of the Sun.

constellation-057.summary: The barred spiral galaxy that contains our solar system, seen as a hazy band across the night sky.
facts: Its disk is about 90,000 light-years across and holds an estimated 100 to 400 billion stars.
The supermassive black hole at its center is about 27,000 light-years away, and its first image was released in 2022.

constellation-058.summary: The larger of two neighboring galaxies, hanging like a hazy smudge in the southern sky.
facts: In 1987 a supernova exploded here that could be seen with the naked eye.
It got its name after being described in the records of a round-the-world voyage.

constellation-059.summary: The smaller of two neighboring galaxies hanging in the southern sky.
facts: It's about 200,000 light-years away, yet still visible to the naked eye.
Leavitt's study of its variable stars opened the way to measuring distances across the universe.

constellation-060.summary: One of the largest and brightest star-forming clouds spread across the southern sky.
facts: It contains the extremely massive star Eta Carinae.
It's about four times the size of the Orion Nebula and lies about 8,500 light-years away.
